description: Turkic steppe empire north of the Caucasus (c. 650–969) whose ruling class converted to Judaism in the eighth century in a unique act of confessional state formation; its position between Byzantine, Abbasid, and later Viking spheres made it the keystone of Eurasian commercial and diplomatic networks before Sviatoslav of Kiev's campaign destroyed the khaganate.

temporal.notes: Steppe empire with notable Jewish religious adoption; defeated by Sviatoslav

lifecycle_phases.description: Khazars control the Pontic-Caspian steppe between the Caucasus and the Volga, blocking Arab expansion northward. The famous conversion of the Khazar elite to Judaism (c.740) creates a unique religious identity, the only medieval Jewish-ruled polity. Serve as a crucial buffer protecting Byzantine and early Rus lands from Umayyad raids.

Rus raids from the north weaken Khazar commercial dominance of Volga trade. Sviatoslav of Kiev destroys the Khazar capital Sarkel (965) and captures Itil; the Khaganate rapidly collapses, replaced by the Pechenegs on the steppe.

rise_factors.description: Khazar control of Volga and Caspian trade routes connected the Silk Road to Scandinavia via the Rus river network; toll revenues from this trade made the Khazar capital Itil one of the wealthiest cities of the early medieval period

Khazaria's steppe heartland and Caucasus mountain flank created a natural strategic position that blocked Arab armies from expanding north of the Caucasus; Byzantine alliance provided diplomatic and material support

The Khazars controlled the lower Volga and Don river crossings, the main overland route between Central Asia and the Black Sea. Toll revenues from Silk Road trade made Itil (Atil) one of the wealthiest cities of the early medieval world.

Khazar armies defeated the Umayyad Caliphate twice (627, 730) in the Caucasus, halting Arab expansion into Eastern Europe. Medieval Islamic chronicles acknowledged the Khazars as the northern limit of the caliphate's effective power.
The Khagan's conversion to Judaism (c. 740) positioned the state as religiously neutral between Christian Byzantium and Islamic caliphates, enabling trade with both without political subordination.

The Khazar royal house's conversion to Judaism in the 8th century gave the khaganate a unique religious identity that allowed it to act as a neutral buffer between Christian Byzantium and Islamic Caliphates without being absorbed into either sphere.

decline_factors.description: Kievan Rus emerged as a competing power controlling northern Volga trade; Sviatoslav's military campaigns (965–969) systematically destroyed Khazar fortified positions and opened the trade routes to direct Rus control

The dual kingship system (sacred Khagan and functional Bek) created structural governance tensions; by the 900s the institution had weakened without developing administrative alternatives to nomadic personal rule
Sviatoslav I of Kiev systematically destroyed the Khazar state (965–969): sacking Sarkel, Itil, and Semender in rapid succession, eliminating Khazar military capacity and commercial infrastructure.

Khazar governance split authority between a sacred khagan (spiritual/symbolic king) and a bek (military commander). This dual-authority system created persistent succession disputes and weakened unified decision-making.

sources.author: Golden, Peter B.
sources.title: Khazar Studies: A Historico-Philological Inquiry into the Origins of the Khazars
